column5: Moses writes covenant words
column6: The commentary names Moses as recipient of the first pages; after Sinai, Moses writes the LORD's words in a book, locating the written witness in Moses' own scriptural story.

column5: Book of the Covenant read aloud
column6: The commentary links old pages to a recited teaching; here Moses reads the written covenant in the people's hearing, and they answer by undertaking to obey it.

column5: Moses completes the written Torah
column6: The commentary says the current warning is already in ancient pages; this verse explicitly says Moses completed writing the words of the Torah in a book.

column5: Book kept as a witness
column6: The commentary calls the first pages a witness against the charge of novelty; Moses orders the completed book placed beside the ark as a witness against Israel, giving the text a future-testimony role.

column5: Public reading of the Torah
column6: The commentary connects scripture with a message heard rather than a page handed to the Prophet; Moses orders the Torah read aloud before all Israel at the appointed gathering.

column5: All Israel hears and learns
column6: The commentary's pages preserve instruction for later hearers; this assembly includes men, women, children, and resident aliens so they hear, learn, and fear the LORD.

column5: Children learn through hearing
column6: The commentary says the word reaches a later generation without the Prophet consulting a page; Moses specifically includes children who have not known the Torah, so they hear and learn it.

column5: Reading with explanation
column6: The commentary presents recitation as the means by which written teaching becomes present to hearers; in Nehemiah, Levites read from the Torah and explain its sense so the assembly understands.

column5: Jeremiah dictates a scroll
column6: The commentary contrasts old written pages with the Prophet's received recitation; Jeremiah dictates the LORD's words and Baruch writes them on a scroll, making the prophet's speech a written document.

column5: Baruch reads the scroll publicly
column6: The commentary joins ancient pages to audible proclamation; Baruch reads Jeremiah's scroll in the temple before the gathered people and officials.

column5: The burned words are rewritten
column6: The commentary says the teaching endured from the first pages to its present recitation; after Jehoiakim burns the scroll, Jeremiah is told to write the same words again, showing the message surviving destruction of its copy.

column5: A vision made readable
column6: The commentary pictures old writing as an open, legible surface; Habakkuk is told to write the vision plainly on tablets so a reader can run with it, explicitly joining a written revelation to its public transmission.

column5: Words kept in the heart
column6: The commentary says the pages' message reaches the Prophet as recitation and is retained; Moses commands Israel to keep these words in the heart, joining scripture with inward memory.

column5: Words recited to children
column6: The commentary treats the old teaching as a living word heard by later people; Deuteronomy requires parents to teach and speak it at home, on the road, at bedtime, and at rising.

column5: What fathers heard is told onward
column6: The commentary answers the claim that the message is new by locating it among earlier generations; the psalm says its teaching was heard and known from the fathers who told it.

column5: The next generation is not left ignorant
column6: The commentary says an ancient warning remains present rather than forgotten; the psalm refuses to hide the fathers' praise-worthy acts from their children and pledges to tell the next generation.

column5: Remembering leads to trust and obedience
column6: The commentary links recited remembrance to fear of God and the surah's counsel; Psalm 78 says the next generation should hope in God, not forget his works, and keep his commands.

column5: Ask the elders about days of old
column6: The commentary answers “we never heard this from our ancestors” by asserting ancient continuity; Moses tells the audience to remember former days and ask their fathers and elders.

column5: The word is near, in mouth and heart
column6: The commentary says the Prophet receives the pages' content by recitation rather than by handling them; Deuteronomy describes the commandment as near, in the hearer's mouth and heart, ready to be done.

column5: God's word outlasts fading life
column6: The commentary says the world passes but the statement about the lasting hereafter has itself endured; Isaiah contrasts withering grass and flowers with God's word standing forever.

column5: The word fixed forever
column6: The commentary treats the first pages as a durable witness across generations; the psalm says God's word is established in heaven forever, supplying a concrete scriptural image of permanence.

column5: A book of remembrance for the God-fearing
column6: The commentary connects fear of God, remembrance, and preserved pages; Malachi describes those who fear the LORD speaking together while a book of remembrance is written before him for them.

column5: Prophetic words sealed for the end
column6: The commentary says the first writing bears witness to the final outcome; Daniel is told to shut up and seal the words until the time of the end, a different but concrete model of an ancient text preserved for a later age.

column5: Each person answers for their own sin
column6: The commentary joins self-purification to the saying that no bearer carries another's burden; Deuteronomy's legal rule says parent and child are not executed for one another's sin, but each for their own.

column5: A child does not bear a parent's iniquity
column6: The commentary reads purification as one's own act and cites the rule that none bears another's load; Ezekiel explicitly assigns guilt to the person who sins, not to that person's father or son.

column5: Turning from sin brings life
column6: The commentary's “one who purifies himself” is an individual turning toward good; Ezekiel says the person who turns from transgression, keeps the statutes, and does right shall live.

column5: Each dies for their own iniquity
column6: The commentary's cited page teaching denies transferred burdens; Jeremiah answers the sour-grapes proverb by saying each person dies for their own iniquity, sharpening the move from inherited blame to individual responsibility.

column5: Fear God and keep the commandments
column6: The commentary's nearby verses join fearing God, purification, and prayer to the choice of the hereafter; Ecclesiastes closes by making fear of God and keeping his commandments the whole human duty.

column5: Every deed comes to judgment
column6: The commentary places the more enduring hereafter against present preference; Ecclesiastes grounds that contrast in God's judgment of every deed, including what is hidden.

column5: Awakening to everlasting life
column6: The commentary says the hereafter is better and more enduring than present life; Daniel's sleepers awake, some to everlasting life and others to disgrace, giving that future a resurrection setting.

column5: Wealth cannot follow at death
column6: The commentary challenges preferring the near life to the lasting one; Psalm 49 says a person takes nothing from wealth at death and that splendor does not descend after him.

column5: The wicked choose immediate pleasure
column6: The commentary rejects preferring the present life because the hereafter is more enduring; Wisdom 2 puts the opposite case in the mouths of the wicked, who urge one another to enjoy present goods and youth.

column5: The righteous are safe beyond apparent death
column6: The commentary says the afterlife is the better, abiding outcome; Wisdom says the souls of the righteous are in God's hand and seem only to have died, directly overturning a worldly judgment of their fate.

column5: A martyr chooses resurrection over survival
column6: The commentary says the later life is better than the near one; the second brother accepts death under torture while confessing that the King of the world will raise the faithful to renewed life.

column5: Hope beyond death
column6: The commentary makes the enduring hereafter the reason not to privilege present life; the fourth brother says he hopes to be raised by God, while his persecutor has no share in resurrection to life.

column5: The world passes; God's will remains
column6: The commentary contrasts the passing world with what is more enduring; John says the world and its desire are passing away, while the one who does God's will remains forever.

column5: Moses values the future reward above Egypt
column6: The commentary names Moses' pages as a source for rejecting worldly preference; Hebrews depicts Moses refusing Egypt's treasures and choosing reproach because he was looking to the reward.

column5: The whole world cannot outweigh life
column6: The commentary asks why one would prefer the near world over the lasting hereafter; Jesus asks what profit it is to gain the whole world and forfeit one's life.

column5: Treasure that does not decay
column6: The commentary calls the hereafter more enduring than worldly life; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven, where moth and rust do not destroy it.

column5: Visible things are temporary
column6: The commentary says the world passes while the message about the hereafter lasts; Paul contrasts what is seen and temporary with what is unseen and eternal.

column5: Earlier writings teach and sustain hope
column6: The commentary says 87:18 answers novelty by locating its teaching in first pages; Paul says what was written in former times was written for present instruction and endurance, to give hope.

column5: Ancient events written for later admonition
column6: The commentary treats old pages as a warning to present hearers who prefer the world; Paul says the earlier events occurred as examples and were written down for admonition of later generations.

column5: Scripture preached beforehand to Abraham
column6: The commentary names Abraham among the recipients of the first pages; Paul reads Genesis as scripture foreseeing the Gentiles' justification and announcing the gospel beforehand to Abraham.

column5: Moses' writing witnesses to a later message
column6: The commentary answers that the present teaching is not a new invention by naming Moses' pages; Jesus says Moses wrote about him, making the older Torah a witness to a later proclamation and criticizing hearers who reject both.

column5: Paul claims continuity with Moses and the prophets
column6: The commentary's central claim is that the current warning was already in ancient pages; Paul tells Agrippa that he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets said would happen.

column5: Scripture known from childhood guides salvation
column6: The commentary describes an old text whose recited teaching still instructs its hearers; Timothy's sacred writings, known from childhood, are said to make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ.

column5: Flesh fades like grass
column6: The commentary's adjacent claim is that worldly life passes while its message endures; Peter compares all flesh to grass and its glory to a flower that falls.

column5: The preached word endures
column6: The commentary says the ancient pages' statement has survived to the Prophet's recitation; Peter says the Lord's word remains forever and identifies it with the gospel preached to his readers.

column5: The dead judged from opened books
column6: The commentary links pages, deeds, and the eventual outcome; Revelation depicts books opened at judgment and the dead judged according to what was written in them and what they had done.

column5: Each carries their own load
column6: The commentary's reading of purification is personal and is paired with “no bearer bears another's burden”; Paul says each person will carry their own load.

column5: Each gives an account to God
column6: The commentary connects the old pages' warning with each person's own conduct; Paul says each of us will give an account of himself to God.

column5: Each receives for deeds done in the body
column6: The commentary links personal purification and the enduring hereafter; Paul says all must appear before Christ's judgment seat so each may receive for what was done in the body.

column5: God repays according to deeds
column6: The commentary pairs individual action with the coming outcome; Paul says God will repay each person according to their deeds, explicitly connecting conduct and judgment.

column5: Eternal life for those seeking what lasts
column6: The commentary says the afterlife is better and more enduring; Paul specifies eternal life for those who persevere in good work while seeking glory, honor, and immortality.

column5: Hope purifies the hopeful person
column6: The commentary says the successful person “purifies himself”; John uses the same reflexive moral pattern, saying everyone with this hope purifies himself as Christ is pure.

column5: Clean hands and purified hearts
column6: The commentary joins purification to remembrance of God and prayer; James calls those drawing near to God to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts.

column5: Prayer with unclean hands is rejected
column6: The commentary places purification beside remembering God's name and prayer; Isaiah depicts worshippers spreading hands in prayer, but God refuses to hear because their hands are full of blood.

column5: Wash and make yourselves clean
column6: The commentary says the person who purifies himself succeeds; Isaiah's answer to corrupt worship is a concrete command to wash and cleanse, then cease doing evil.

column5: Purity expressed as justice
column6: The commentary links purification and prayer, not mere ritual display; Isaiah specifies learning good, seeking justice, and defending the vulnerable as the ethical turn that follows cleansing.

column5: God brings grass up for cattle
column6: The commentary links the surah's opening pasture to Moses' description of God sending rain and bringing out plants; the psalm says God makes grass grow for livestock and plants for human use.

column5: Moses and the prophets already speak
column6: The commentary says people asking for new sheets lack fear, since the old pages already give warning; in Jesus' story Abraham answers a dead rich man's request by pointing to Moses and the prophets, which his brothers should hear.

column5: A new sign cannot replace hearing scripture
column6: The commentary says another page would not cure refusal to heed the existing warning; Abraham's reply is that those who will not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by someone rising from the dead.

column5: Fear, love, and service
column6: The commentary joins fear of God to purification and prayer; Moses asks Israel to fear the LORD, walk in his ways, love and serve him with all the heart and soul.

column5: God purifies the heart
column6: The commentary describes a person purifying himself, while Ezekiel and other texts personalize responsibility; Deuteronomy adds that God circumcises the heart so Israel may love him, making divine aid part of inner renewal.

column5: Choose life rather than death
column6: The commentary says hearers prefer the near life despite the better hereafter; Moses sets life and death before Israel and urges them to choose life by loving and clinging to God.

column5: The righteous meditate on Torah continually
column6: The commentary says the old word is recited, remembered, and acted on; Psalm 1 locates the righteous person's delight in the LORD's instruction, meditated on day and night.

column5: Two paths end differently
column6: The commentary's world/hereafter contrast culminates in different outcomes; Psalm 1 says the LORD knows the way of the righteous while the way of the wicked perishes.

column5: Do not envy worldly splendor
column6: The commentary rebukes preference for worldly life; Psalm 49 tells the hearer not to fear when another grows rich and his household's glory increases, setting up the death-boundary made explicit in v.17.

column5: God weighs the heart and repays deeds
column6: The commentary says each person's choice matters and cites the rule that no one bears another's burden; Proverbs answers the excuse “we did not know” by saying the heart-weigher sees and repays each according to work.

column5: Turn and live
column6: The commentary's purification is a person's own turning, not a transferred act; Ezekiel calls the house of Israel to repent and turn from transgressions so iniquity will not be a stumbling block.

column5: Remember Moses' Torah before the coming day
column6: The commentary names Moses' pages and says their teaching addresses the final outcome; Malachi closes by telling Israel to remember the Torah commanded to Moses at Horeb before the coming day of the LORD.

column5: The end announced from the beginning
column6: The commentary says the first pages already tell where all things will end; Isaiah portrays God as declaring the end from the beginning and bringing his purpose to completion.

column5: Moses' book leads the successor
column6: The commentary pictures the first writings as going ahead and later speech following their path; Joshua, Moses' successor, is told to keep the Torah book in his mouth, meditate on it, and act according to it.

column5: Abraham obeys God's commandments
column6: The commentary names Abraham as recipient of ancient pages; Genesis says Abraham obeyed God's voice and kept his charge, commandments, statutes, and instructions, giving a concrete ancestral precedent for the teaching.

column5: Abraham's faith counted as righteousness
column6: The commentary names Abraham among the first recipients; Genesis presents Abraham believing God and being counted righteous, the verse Paul later treats as an early scriptural witness to faith.

column5: Abraham keeps the law and covenant
column6: The commentary's final verse names Abraham and Moses together; Ben Sira remembers Abraham as keeping the law of the Most High and entering a covenant, showing a Jewish retelling that makes him a model of ancient fidelity.

column5: Moses' memory is praised
column6: The commentary names Moses as bearer of the old pages; Ben Sira's praise of the ancestors turns to Moses as beloved by God and honored, adding a Jewish wisdom portrait of the named lawgiver.

column5: Abraham observed Torah before Sinai
column6: The commentary's “first pages” include Abraham as well as Moses; this midrash reads Genesis 26:5 to say Abraham kept the Torah before it was given, extending the antiquity of revealed practice to the patriarch.

column5: Abraham's obedience rendered as Torah observance
column6: The commentary names Abraham's pages but leaves their contents open; Onqelos renders the Genesis account in terms of Abraham keeping God's commandments and teachings, giving an Aramaic interpretive bridge from the patriarch to Torah.

column5: A ledger records every deed
column6: The commentary connects enduring pages with personal accountability; Avot pictures an open book and a recording hand alongside judgment, making written record a rabbinic image for the moral accounting implied by the pages.

column5: Heavenly tablets record human deeds
column6: The commentary says a divine book preserves what happened to the first generations; Enoch is shown heavenly tablets and reads what is written there, an apocalyptic expansion of memory and record beyond earthly pages.

column5: The righteous are remembered in books
column6: The commentary links fearers and a preserved record; Enoch depicts the books of the righteous and their prayers brought before the Lord of Spirits, a Jewish apocalyptic counterpart to a heavenly book of remembrance.

column5: A bounded ancient scriptural collection
column6: The commentary answers that the message is not a new invention by locating it in first pages; Josephus defends the antiquity and counted extent of Jewish sacred books, showing how a Jewish author argued for a stable inherited corpus.

column5: Christian religion claimed as ancient
column6: The commentary answers novelty by saying the teaching was present in the first pages; Augustine argues that what is now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients from the beginning, a patristic reading of present faith as recovery rather than late invention.

column5: Purity by guarding the word
column6: The commentary joins self-purification to the recited old teaching; Psalm 119 asks how a young person's way can be kept pure and answers by guarding it according to God's word.

column5: The word stored in the heart
column6: The commentary says revelation reaches the Prophet by recitation and is not forgotten; the psalmist stores God's word in the heart to avoid sin, linking remembered scripture with moral purification.

column5: Clean hands and a pure heart in worship
column6: The commentary joins purification to prayer; the psalm describes the one who may ascend God's holy place as having clean hands and a pure heart, tying inward and outward purity to worship.

column5: A prayer for a clean heart
column6: The commentary describes the person who purifies himself; David asks God to create a clean heart in him, adding a distinct emphasis on purification received from God rather than self-congratulation.

column5: A lost Torah scroll is rediscovered
column6: The commentary says first-page teaching endured into the present; in Kings, Hilkiah finds a Torah book in the temple after it had been absent from the king's practice, and its recovery prompts reform, complicating any simple picture of uninterrupted access.

column5: A king burns the scroll
column6: The commentary says the old word has lasted; Jeremiah's scroll is cut and burned by Jehoiakim, a concrete counter-image of the vulnerability of the physical page before the message is rewritten in v.28.

column5: The righteous' hope is full of immortality
column6: The commentary calls the hereafter more enduring than this life; Wisdom says the righteous may seem punished at death, yet their hope is full of immortality, correcting the worldly reading of their fate.

column5: Those who trust God abide with him
column6: The commentary calls the later life more enduring; Wisdom says those who trust God will understand truth and abide with him in love, specifying the lasting communion behind its reversal of worldly judgment.

column5: Prayer, fasting, and almsgiving together
column6: The commentary pairs purification and prayer and its refs mention prayer with almsgiving; Tobit says prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving, giving a Jewish ethical-worship combination rather than treating prayer as an isolated rite.

column5: Treasure laid up for the future life
column6: The commentary contrasts present worldly preference with the lasting hereafter; Paul tells the rich to store up treasure as a foundation for the future and take hold of the life that is truly life.

column5: Riches gathered only for oneself do not last
column6: The commentary warns against preferring the near life; Jesus' rich fool stores goods for himself but dies that night, and the story calls him poor toward God.

column5: The patriarchs seek a better country
column6: The commentary names Abraham among the first pages and says the hereafter is better; Hebrews reads the patriarchs as desiring a better, heavenly country and a city prepared by God.

column5: The gospel promised beforehand in scripture
column6: The commentary's claim is that the present word is already in the earliest writings; Paul introduces the gospel as promised beforehand through God's prophets in holy scriptures.

column5: Moses and the prophets interpreted as witnesses
column6: The commentary says the recent teaching is contained in earlier pages; Luke depicts Jesus interpreting what the scriptures say about him, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, a Christian rereading of the old texts as testimony to the present.

column5: A written prophecy declared fulfilled in hearing
column6: The commentary joins pages to a word heard in the present; after reading Isaiah in the synagogue, Jesus says the scripture has been fulfilled in the hearers' hearing.

column5: Earlier prophets searched the promised grace
column6: The commentary says the first pages already contain the later warning; Peter describes prophets who searched and inquired about the grace now announced, connecting prior revelation with a later proclamation.

column5: Earlier prophets served later hearers
column6: The commentary says the old word has reached the Prophet's audience; Peter says the prophets were serving not themselves but later readers, to whom the gospel is now announced.

column5: A letter read in human hearts
column6: The commentary says the pages' content can be present without a page in the Prophet's hand; Paul calls the Corinthians a letter known and read by all, a human community serving as written testimony.

column5: Writing by the Spirit on hearts
column6: The commentary contrasts a physical page with a message recited and retained; Paul says the Spirit writes on tablets of human hearts rather than stone, developing a Christian image of inwardly carried scripture.

column5: God spoke formerly through prophets
column6: The commentary says the same enduring warning was present in older pages; Hebrews describes God speaking to ancestors through prophets in many times and ways, then frames the present as a further stage of that speech.

column5: Self-cleansing perfected in fear of God
column6: The commentary joins purification with fear and prayer; Paul urges believers to cleanse themselves from defilement and perfect holiness in fear of God, an explicit ethical counterpart to the surah's purifier who fears.

column5: The repentant prayer is accepted over self-display
column6: The commentary warns that self-purification is not self-praise; Jesus' parable ends with the tax collector, not the self-congratulating Pharisee, going home justified, clarifying the difference between turning toward God and claiming one's own merit.

column5: Moses' signs and Pharaoh's magicians
column6: The commentary cites opponents of Moses calling his clear signs fabricated magic and unheard by their ancestors; Exodus stages a Moses-and-Pharaoh sign contest in which Pharaoh's magicians answer with their arts, a related scene framed as rival performance rather than ancestral novelty.

column5: The recovered book is read to the king
column6: The commentary presents the ancient pages as a witness to the present; the king's secretary reads the rediscovered Torah book to Josiah, but the episode concerns recovery after neglect, so the link is about renewed hearing rather than uninterrupted preservation.

column5: Write and recite to Joshua
column6: The commentary joins preserved pages to a word received and recited; God tells Moses both to write the Amalek remembrance in a book and to recite it in Joshua's hearing, combining writing, memory, and oral succession.

column5: The king makes a copy of the Torah
column6: The commentary says the old pages guide present conduct; Deuteronomy requires a king to write a copy of the Torah, making the text a concrete guide for a later ruler.

column5: The king reads the Torah throughout life
column6: The commentary warns against preferring the near world's status; the king must read his copy all his life to learn fear of God and avoid exalting himself over his kin.

column5: A written song taught by heart as witness
column6: The commentary links ancient pages with recitation and remembrance; Moses is told to write a song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths as a witness for later generations.

column5: The song witnesses when Israel forgets
column6: The commentary says a lasting divine record stands against neglect of the warning; Deuteronomy anticipates Israel's later turning away and says the taught song will testify because it will not be forgotten by their descendants.

column5: Teach the remembered revelation to descendants
column6: The commentary answers “we did not hear this from our ancestors” by asserting an ancient message; Moses warns Israel not to forget what it saw at Horeb and to make it known to children and grandchildren.

column5: Words of prophecy written in a book
column6: The commentary says the current recitation is already in ancient pages; Jeremiah is specifically commanded to write all the words spoken to him in a book, preserving a prophetic message for later hearers.

column5: A book as a witness for future time
column6: The commentary describes old pages as a public witness to a present warning; Isaiah is told to write the message on a tablet and in a book so it may stand for a future day as a witness forever.

column5: Words remain in mouths across generations
column6: The commentary says the first-pages message has endured to the Prophet's recitation; Isaiah promises that God's words placed in the speaker's mouth will not depart from him, his children, or descendants.

column5: Torah written on the heart
column6: The commentary says the page's teaching is heard and retained inwardly; Jeremiah's new-covenant promise places God's Torah within the people and writes it on their hearts, an inward counterpart to external pages.

column5: A record written for a future generation
column6: The commentary says the message survives from the first pages to present readers; the psalm explicitly says a future generation will praise the LORD and that this should be written down for a people yet to be created.

column5: A scroll written on both sides
column6: The commentary asks the reader to picture a separate written sheet rather than a bound codex; Ezekiel sees an opened scroll written on its front and back, a striking prophetic image of a densely inscribed surface.

column5: The prophet eats the scroll and speaks its words
column6: The commentary says pages reach the Prophet as an inwardly retained recitation rather than as a page in his hand; Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll and then speak its words to Israel, a bodily enactment of internalized prophecy.

column5: Books opened at the court of judgment
column6: The commentary links ancient pages with the final accounting of deeds; Daniel's heavenly court sits and books are opened, a Jewish apocalyptic scene of written records at judgment.

column5: The delivered are found written in the book
column6: The commentary says the first generations are not lost because their knowledge is kept in a book with God; Daniel speaks of those found written in the book being delivered at the final crisis.

column5: The world fades while salvation lasts
column6: The commentary contrasts the passing world with a teaching that endures; Isaiah says heaven and earth will wear away like clothing while God's salvation and righteousness remain forever.

column5: Guided now and received to glory afterward
column6: The commentary joins divine guidance in the surah's opening to the claim that the final destination is with the Lord; the psalmist says God guides him by counsel and afterward receives him to glory.

column5: God remains when flesh fails
column6: The commentary says the hereafter is more enduring than worldly life; the psalmist's flesh and heart may fail, but God is his portion forever, a personal formulation of lasting hope.

column5: God receives the speaker from Sheol
column6: The commentary says the afterlife is better and more enduring than the present; Psalm 49 contrasts the rich man's death with the speaker's confidence that God will ransom and receive him from Sheol.

column5: Not abandoned to Sheol
column6: The commentary's “more enduring” hereafter entails a future beyond death; the psalmist trusts not to be abandoned to Sheol or left to see the Pit, giving that hope a resurrection-shaped expression.

column5: The path of life ends in lasting joy
column6: The commentary says the final arrival is with the Lord; Psalm 16 speaks of the path of life and fullness of joy in God's presence forever.

column5: The blameless inherit what lasts
column6: The commentary sets present worldly preference against the enduring hereafter; Psalm 37 says the days of the blameless are known to God and their inheritance endures forever.

column5: Purification expressed as freeing the oppressed
column6: The commentary pairs purification with prayer and cites almsgiving alongside it; Isaiah's chosen fast is to loosen injustice and free the oppressed, giving purification an ethical and social form.

column5: Share bread and shelter the poor
column6: The commentary's nearby purification and prayer are also associated with giving; Isaiah continues by naming bread shared with the hungry, shelter for the homeless, and clothing for the naked as the fast God desires.

column5: Pure religion keeps unstained from the world
column6: The commentary joins purification to worship and warns against preferring worldly life; James defines pure and undefiled religion by care for vulnerable people and keeping oneself unstained by the world.

column5: Alms become treasure that does not fail
column6: The commentary's references connect purification with giving and the hereafter with lasting reward; Jesus tells disciples to sell possessions, give alms, and make a heavenly purse that does not wear out.

column5: Present affliction produces lasting glory
column6: The commentary contrasts a passing worldly life with what endures; Paul calls present affliction momentary and light in comparison with the eternal weight of glory it produces.

column5: Present suffering is outweighed by future glory
column6: The commentary says the afterlife is better than the near life; Paul says present sufferings are not worth comparing with the glory that will be revealed, giving the contrast an explicit scale.

column5: Hope limited to this life is inadequate
column6: The commentary challenges those who prefer worldly life and dismiss the hereafter; Paul argues that if hope in Christ were only for this life, believers would be most pitiable, directly rejecting a this-world-only horizon.

column5: “Eat and drink” is the rival response to death
column6: The commentary's opponents prefer the near life over the lasting one; in an argument for resurrection Paul cites the maxim to eat and drink because tomorrow one dies, presenting it as the consequence of denying resurrection.

column5: Scoffers appeal to what has always been
column6: The commentary answers novelty and skepticism by saying the final warning was already in the first pages; Peter's scoffers ask where the promised coming is and claim everything has continued as from the beginning of creation.

column5: The promised day still arrives
column6: The commentary says the oldest pages already announce the final outcome; Peter says the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly, carrying the passage's answer to scoffers into its own conclusion.

column5: A prophetic charge of scribal distortion
column6: The commentary cites the concealment of parts of earlier books but says this teaching is truly in the first pages; Jeremiah's own context accuses scribes of making the LORD's Torah into a lie, a sharp counter-witness about the handling of scripture.

column5: Joshua reads Moses' law to the assembly
column6: The commentary pictures the first writing leading later generations; after Moses, Joshua reads the Torah's blessings and curses before all Israel, a distinct public scene of a successor carrying the earlier book forward.

column5: No word is omitted from the public reading
column6: The commentary says the pages' teaching is available in the recited message; Joshua leaves out no word of Moses' command before the whole assembly, including women, children, and resident aliens.

column5: The people attend to a long public reading
column6: The commentary makes the heard word central to access to old pages; Ezra reads the Torah aloud from morning until midday before the gathered people, whose ears are attentive.

column5: The word from God's mouth accomplishes its purpose
column6: The commentary says the old-page statement has endured into present recitation; Isaiah adds that God's word does not return empty but accomplishes what God intends, explaining the active effect of a message that is heard.

column5: Peter reads a psalm as prophecy of resurrection
column6: The commentary says the first pages already tell of the final destination with God; Peter interprets David's words about not being abandoned to Hades as a prophecy of the Messiah's resurrection.

column5: Torah passes through a named chain
column6: The commentary pictures the earliest pages leading the later word; Avot opens by tracing Torah from Moses at Sinai through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the Great Assembly, a rabbinic account of transmission across generations.

column5: Self-responsibility balanced by obligations to others
column6: The commentary stresses that a person purifies himself and no one bears another's burden; Hillel asks who will act for a person if he does not act for himself, then warns against living only for oneself.

column5: This world as a vestibule to the world to come
column6: The commentary says the later life is better and more enduring than the present; Avot compares this world to a vestibule and the world to come to the banquet hall, urging preparation in the former.

column5: Books of judgment opened at the year's beginning
column6: The commentary links preserved pages and personal deeds; the Talmud describes books opened for the righteous, wicked, and intermediate, developing a Jewish tradition of recorded moral standing and judgment.

column5: A father hands written books to descendants
column6: The commentary says what was written for the first generations reaches a later reciter; Enoch tells Methuselah to preserve the books received from his father's hand and pass them to generations of the world.

column5: Public books restored after loss
column6: The commentary says an ancient message is still present in the recited Qur'an; Ezra's apocalyptic account says the twenty-four books he has written are to be made public for worthy and unworthy readers, a tradition of textual restoration and access.

column5: Law, prophets, and psalms all bear witness
column6: The commentary says the present teaching is in the earliest pages; Jesus identifies what is written about him in Moses' law, prophets, and psalms as needing fulfillment, an explicit Christian claim that the old corpus anticipates later events.

column5: Deuteronomy's near word becomes proclaimed faith
column6: The commentary says the Prophet receives the message orally and that the pages' content is present in recitation; Paul quotes Deuteronomy's word near the mouth and heart as the word of faith he proclaims, giving the old verse a new Christian referent.

column5: Hearers test a new proclamation against scripture
column6: The commentary answers the charge that the current word is novel by pointing to older pages; the Bereans receive Paul's message eagerly but examine the scriptures daily to see whether his claims hold.

column5: A promise made to the fathers is now announced
column6: The commentary says the old pages contain the current warning; Paul tells the synagogue that he is bringing good news of what God promised to the fathers.

column5: The fathers' promise interpreted as fulfilled now
column6: The commentary argues that the present word confirms an earlier one; Paul says God fulfilled the promise to their descendants by raising Jesus and supports the claim with a psalm.

column5: Paul interprets Abraham's belief as counted righteousness
column6: The commentary names Abraham among the recipients of the first pages; Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 to make Abraham's belief a scriptural example of righteousness by faith, a distinct reading from Galatians' “gospel preached beforehand.”

column5: Jesus claims fulfillment rather than abolition
column6: The commentary answers that its teaching is not new by locating it in the first pages; Jesus says he came not to abolish the law or prophets but to fulfill them, making continuity an explicit claim.

column5: The scriptures testify, yet hearers refuse to come
column6: The commentary says the old pages already contain the warning and lack of response is the problem; Jesus says the searched scriptures testify about him, while his hearers will not come to him for life.

column5: The same God speaks in the last days through the Son
column6: The commentary's “first” pages carry a message about the final outcome; Hebrews contrasts God's former speech through prophets with his speech in these last days through the Son, holding continuity and changed mode together.

column5: Abraham obeys and leaves without knowing the destination
column6: The commentary names Abraham among the ancient recipients; Hebrews recalls his obedient departure by faith, showing the patriarch's own response to a divine word as part of the scriptural precedent.

column5: The end speaks of first, last, beginning, and end
column6: The commentary says the first pages already disclose where all things finally arrive; Revelation names the speaker as Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end, a Christian formula joining origin to final outcome.

column5: Salvation is gift, not grounds for boasting
column6: The commentary stresses personal purification and responsibility; Paul says salvation is by grace through faith, not from works, adding a Christian boundary against reading moral self-purification as earning rescue.

column5: Grace issues in a life of good works
column6: The commentary does not equate personal action with boasting; Paul continues that those saved by grace are created in Christ for good works, preserving ethical action while denying that it is self-earned salvation.

column5: One person's act has consequences for many
column6: The commentary's cited rule says no one bears another's burden; Paul says one man's disobedience made many sinners and one man's obedience makes many righteous, a distinct corporate account of consequence rather than a simple transfer of personal guilt.

column5: Letter and Spirit set in interpretive contrast
column6: The commentary holds together physical pages and a word received inwardly; Paul contrasts the letter that kills with the Spirit that gives life in a discussion of the new covenant, adding a Christian interpretive tension without making him reject scripture.
